title: LLM Fundamentals and Decoding Strategies
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# LLM Fundamentals and Decoding Strategies ##### The model that got stuck saying "thank you for your patience" A support-automation team in Gurugram shipped an LLM-drafted reply feature. In testing it was fine. In production, roughly one reply in forty degenerated into a loop: > "Thank you for your patience. Thank you for your patience. Thank you for your patience..." They assumed the model was broken and considered switching providers. The model was fine. Their config had `do_sample=False`, which means greedy decoding — always take the highest-probability token. Holtzman et al. documented exactly this failure in *The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration*: maximum-likelihood decoding on open-ended text reliably collapses into repetition, because once a phrase appears, the model's own context makes repeating it the single most probable continuation. Changing three parameters — `do_sample=True, top_p=0.9, temperature=0.7` — eliminated the problem entirely. No retraining, no provider switch. Decoding is not a detail you leave at defaults. It is a control surface as consequential as the model choice. ##### Autoregressive generation An LLM is a function from a token sequence to a probability distribution over the next token: ``` P(x₁, x₂, …, x_n) = ∏ P(x_t | x₁, …, x_{t−1}) ``` Generation is a loop: forward pass, get logits over the vocabulary (32k–256k entries), convert to a token, append, repeat. Every token requires a full forward pass through every layer. That single fact explains most of LLM serving economics — the model is the same cost per token whether it is producing brilliance or a loop. Two distinct phases with very different performance characteristics: - **Prefill:** process the whole prompt in one parallel pass. Compute-bound, highly efficient, one big matmul. - **Decode:** generate one token at a time. **Memory-bandwidth-bound** — the entire model's weights must be read from HBM for each single token. This is why generation is slow and why batching helps so dramatically (the weight read is amortised across the batch). ##### Greedy and beam search **Greedy** takes `argmax` every step. Deterministic, fast, and myopic — a locally-optimal token can foreclose a much better continuation. For open-ended text it produces the degeneration above. **Beam search** keeps the k highest-scoring partial sequences at each step, so it can recover from a locally-bad-but-globally-good choice. ```python outputs = model.generate( **inputs, num_beams=4, length_penalty=1.0, # >1 favours longer, <1 favours shorter early_stopping=True, no_repeat_ngram_size=3, max_new_tokens=128, ) ``` The scoring uses length-normalised log-probability, `(1/|y|^α) Σ log P`, because raw log-probability always favours shorter sequences (every additional token multiplies in a probability < 1). The key insight from Holtzman's work: **high-probability text is not human-like text.** Human writing has variable, sometimes surprising word choices; the highest-probability sequence is bland and repetitive. So beam search is excellent for tasks with a genuinely correct answer — translation, summarisation, code, structured extraction — and actively bad for creative or conversational generation. ##### Temperature, top-k, top-p **Temperature** rescales the logits before softmax: `P(x) = softmax(logits / T)`. ```python import numpy as np def apply_temperature(logits, T): if T == 0: out = np.zeros_like(logits); out[logits.argmax()] = 1.0; return out z = logits / T z = z - z.max() # numerical stability e = np.exp(z) return e / e.sum() logits = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5, 0.1]) for T in [0.2, 0.7, 1.0, 1.5]: p = apply_temperature(logits, T) print(f"T={T}: {np.round(p, 3)}") # T=0.2 -> [0.993 0.007 0.000 0.000 0.000] near-deterministic # T=1.5 -> [0.395 0.203 0.104 0.075 0.050] flatter, more surprising ``` T < 1 sharpens toward the mode; T > 1 flattens toward uniform. Temperature alone is a blunt instrument — raising it to increase diversity also raises the chance of sampling genuinely absurd tokens from the tail. **Top-k** truncates to the k most likely tokens, renormalises, then samples. Its weakness is that k is fixed while the appropriate number is not. After "The capital of France is", the distribution is a spike — k=50 forces you to consider 49 wrong answers. After "She opened the door and saw", thousands of continuations are plausible — k=50 is too restrictive. **Top-p (nucleus)** truncates to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds p. The cutoff is **adaptive**: it shrinks to 1–2 tokens where the model is confident and expands to hundreds where it is uncertain. That is exactly the behaviour you want, and it is why top-p is the modern default. ```python def top_p_filter(probs, p=0.9): idx = np.argsort(probs)[::-1] sorted_p = probs[idx] cum = np.cumsum(sorted_p) cutoff = np.searchsorted(cum, p) + 1 # smallest set exceeding p keep = idx[:cutoff] out = np.zeros_like(probs) out[keep] = probs[keep] / probs[keep].sum() return out ``` | Setting | Values | Use for | |---|---|---| | Greedy / T=0 | `do_sample=False` | Classification, extraction, deterministic tests | | Beam search | `num_beams=4` | Translation, summarisation, code completion | | Low sampling | `T=0.3, top_p=0.9` | Factual Q&A, RAG answers | | Balanced | `T=0.7, top_p=0.9` | Chat, general assistance | | High | `T=1.0, top_p=0.95` | Brainstorming, creative writing | Also worth knowing: **min-p** keeps tokens whose probability is at least `min_p × max_prob`, which behaves more robustly than top-p at high temperature and has become popular in local-LLM communities. ##### Repetition penalties and constraints ```python outputs = model.generate( **inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, repetition_penalty=1.1, # divides logits of already-seen tokens no_repeat_ngram_size=4, # hard ban on repeating any 4-gram frequency_penalty=0.3, # OpenAI-style: scales with occurrence count presence_penalty=0.2, # OpenAI-style: flat penalty once seen bad_words_ids=banned_ids, min_new_tokens=20, max_new_tokens=400, ) ``` Use these carefully. `repetition_penalty` above about 1.2 starts degrading fluency, because ordinary function words ("the", "of") legitimately repeat. `no_repeat_ngram_size` is a hard constraint that will break code generation and any text with legitimately repeated structure — never use it for JSON or code. Prefer fixing the underlying cause (switch from greedy to nucleus sampling) over stacking penalties. For hard structural guarantees, **constrained decoding** is the right tool: `outlines`, `guidance`, `lm-format-enforcer` and vLLM's guided decoding mask the logits at each step so only tokens valid under a grammar or JSON schema can be sampled. This makes malformed output structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely. ##### Context windows and the KV cache Each decode step re-attends over all previous tokens. Recomputing their keys and values every step would be O(n²) work. The **KV cache** stores them. ```mermaid flowchart LR A[Prompt: 1200 tokens] --> B[Prefill: one parallel pass
compute + cache K,V for all 1200] B --> C[Decode token 1201:
compute K,V for 1 token, append] C --> D[Attend over 1201 cached K,V] D --> E[Sample token] E --> C ``` The cache turns per-token cost from O(n) recomputation into O(1) appends, but it costs memory: ``` kv_bytes = 2 (K and V) × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × seq_len × batch × dtype_bytes ``` For LLaMA-3-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads via GQA, head_dim 128) in fp16 at 8k context, batch 16: roughly 8.6 GB. Without GQA (32 KV heads) it would be 34 GB. **This is why grouped-query attention exists** — it is a serving optimisation, not a quality one. Techniques built on this: **PagedAttention** (vLLM) manages the cache in fixed-size blocks like OS virtual memory, eliminating fragmentation and enabling copy-on-write prefix sharing; **prefix caching** reuses the cache for a shared system prompt across requests, which can cut time-to-first-token by 80% when every request begins with the same 800-token instruction block; and **KV cache quantisation** to int8 halves the memory for a small quality cost. ##### Tokenization effects Tokenization is where a surprising number of generation bugs originate. **Numbers.** BPE splits digits inconsistently — "1234" might be one token, "1235" two. This is a real contributor to arithmetic errors. Some modern tokenizers force single-digit tokens specifically to fix this. **Indic languages.** Most tokenizers were fit on English-dominant corpora. Devanagari text often costs 3–5× more tokens than equivalent English, which means Hindi or Marathi content hits context limits sooner and costs proportionally more per API call. Always measure token counts on *your* language before budgeting. **The trailing-space trap.** A prompt ending in `"Answer: "` (with a space) is a common bug, because most vocabularies encode words with a leading space (`" Delhi"`). Your trailing space forces the model into an awkward token path and measurably degrades output. **Stop sequences** operate on strings, but generation happens in tokens. If your stop sequence spans a token boundary, it may not trigger. Check `tokenizer.eos_token_id` is set, and validate stop strings against the actual tokenization. ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct") for s in ["Bengaluru", " Bengaluru", "बेंगलुरु", "1234", "1235"]: print(repr(s), tok.encode(s, add_special_tokens=False)) ``` ##### Common mistakes - Greedy decoding on open-ended text, producing degenerate loops. - Beam search for creative or conversational output, producing bland text. - Raising temperature to fix repetition instead of enabling nucleus sampling. - Fixed `top_k` regardless of how peaked the distribution is. - `repetition_penalty` above 1.2, damaging fluency. - `no_repeat_ngram_size` on code or JSON generation. - A trailing space in the prompt. - Ignoring KV cache memory when sizing a deployment, then OOM-ing at long context. - Assuming a 4k context window means 4k English words — for Devanagari it may be 900. - Sampling parameters set once and never evaluated, despite being as impactful as the model choice. ##### Hands-on Take one prompt and generate ten completions under each of six configurations: greedy, beam-4, `T=0.3/top_p=0.9`, `T=0.7/top_p=0.9`, `T=1.2/top_p=0.95`, and `T=0.7/top_k=50`. Measure distinct-3 (fraction of unique trigrams), mean output length, and repetition rate for each, and read a few samples to connect the metrics to what they feel like. Then instrument the loop to print the top-10 token probabilities at three interesting positions. For the mini-project, build a text-generation playground: sliders for temperature, top-k, top-p and repetition penalty; a live bar chart of the top-15 next-token probabilities at each step, showing which tokens the current top-p cutoff includes and excludes; a side-by-side comparison pane for two configurations on the same prompt; and a token-count display that makes the Devanagari-versus-English cost difference visible. Streamlit or Gradio is enough. Then write your top-k-versus-top-p explanation, using a peaked distribution ("The capital of France is") and a flat one ("She opened the door and saw") to show concretely why the adaptive cutoff wins. ##### Key takeaways - Generation is autoregressive: prefill is compute-bound and parallel, decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and sequential. - Maximum-likelihood decoding produces degenerate, repetitive text — high probability is not human-like. - Top-p adapts its cutoff to the model's confidence; that is why it beats fixed top-k as a default. - Use greedy or beam search when there is a correct answer, sampling when there is not; use constrained decoding when structure must be guaranteed. - The KV cache is what makes generation tractable, and its memory footprint is what drives GQA, PagedAttention and prefix caching.
practical_task_reference: Generate text from an open LLM under different decoding settings (greedy, beam, temperature, top-p) and analyze how each changes the output.
mini_project_reference: Build a text-generation playground that exposes decoding parameters and visualizes token probabilities to teach how sampling affects results.
assignment_reference: Explain the difference between top-k and top-p (nucleus) sampling and when each is preferable.
